name: Pan-Arabism
summary: Pan-Arabism holds that the Arabs, bound by one language, history and culture, form a single nation with a natural right to one state from the Atlantic to the Arabian Sea, and that the frontiers between the Arab states are the work of imperialism that unity must remove. Its mainstream, the Ba'th of Aflaq and Nasserism, treats unity, independence from foreign control and rejection of Zionism as one national cause and makes secular, revolutionary and socialist measures part of it; its early liberal and Hashemite strand asked only for independence and unity under a constitutional monarchy.
scope: The mid-20th-century movement for union of the Arab states: the Ba'th (Aflaq, the 1947 constitution, the 1963 congress), Nasserism (Philosophy of the Revolution, the 1962 Charter, speeches to 1966, the 1958 union), the early Arab nationalism recorded by Antonius (1913 Paris Congress, 1919 Syrian Congress), and the League of Arab States Pact and Khartoum resolutions as the state-level foil and consensus. Answers on economy and education rest on the Ba'th constitution and Aflaq, who state socialism and national education as a necessity of the national cause; the wider programmes and practice of the Syrian, Iraqi or Egyptian governments, Syrian-nationalist and local-state nationalisms, and pan-Islamism are excluded.

notes: Strands: the Ba'th and Nasserism were secular-leaning, republican, socialist and anti-Zionist; the early Arab nationalism of 1913-1919 asked for decentralisation, independence and unity under a constitutional monarchy and said nothing on socialism, and the League Pact fixes the existing states. Economic and education answers come only from the Ba'th and Nasser, who state them as part of the national cause, and are medium at most. The main gaps: Husri's own works and Haim's anthology of Arab nationalist texts, Dawisha, Hourani and Cleveland are lending-only on archive.org; Husri's own works and the 1958 UAR provisional constitution could not be opened. Where regimes in power contradicted their words (one-party rule, curbs on opposition), the answer is 0 at low. Themes searched: nation and territory, language and culture, religion and state, Palestine, foreign policy and sovereignty, economy, education, government, means; the doctrine is silent on most of the bank's other statements. Strand pass (2026-10-30): 73 answers had rested only on Ba'th texts. Each was checked against Nasser (Philosophy of the Revolution, the 1962 Charter s13, speeches s6, s7, s12), the 1919 Syrian Congress (s8) and the scholarship (s9, s10, s11): 59 stay where Nasser's Charter or speeches (or the Congress) state the same position, some lowered to the strength the strands share; 4 became splits (0, low) where Nasser holds the opposite or something different (tariffs, class struggle, materialism in history, claims on kin territory); 14 became null because only the Ba'th states them (church-state, scripture as law, conscription, vouchers, uniform civil code, separated powers, history and patriotic teaching, foreign funding, the sacred nation, communal electorates, free college, kin minorities, denominational politics). Education and welfare answers rest on the Ba'th and Nasser only where Nasser states them. The early 1913-1919 strand is silent on most of the economic and social bank. Review (2026-10-30): abolish-central-banks and public-money-creation nulled (bank nationalisation is a nearby case, not the Ba'th state-bank clause).
